where: Section 3, receiver chain, sentence after the bullets: 'Because de-emphasis is a linear filter, putting it on each output after the matrix gives the same result as putting it once on the composite before decoding.'
problem: The claim is wrong. De-emphasis is a real filter with a cut above roughly 2 kHz. Put on the composite, it would act on the difference channel at 38 kHz ± f (23–53 kHz), where its response is a flat, heavy attenuation, not a treble cut. So L − R would come out flat and 20 dB or more weaker, while L + R is properly de-emphasised; the matrix would then give the wrong treble balance. It would also attenuate the 19 kHz pilot before the decoder can lock to it.
fix: De-emphasis must be applied to baseband signals. Because de-emphasis and the matrix are both linear, putting one de-emphasis network on each output after the matrix gives the same result as putting one network on L + R and one on L − R after detection but before the matrix. It is not equivalent to filtering the composite. Also reorder the chain so de-emphasis is listed after the stereo decoder, matching the decoder bullet that already puts a de-emphasis network on each output.

where: Section 3, receiver chain bullet: 'De-emphasis cuts the treble that pre-emphasis boosted, restoring the audio and the noise with it.'
problem: Read literally, this says de-emphasis restores the noise as well as the audio, which is the opposite of what it does. De-emphasis restores flat audio response and at the same time cuts much of the high-frequency noise, which is the main reason pre-emphasis is used.
fix: De-emphasis cuts the treble that pre-emphasis boosted, restoring flat audio response and, at the same time, cutting much of the high-frequency noise picked up in transmission.

problem: 'the receiver would have to filter it out of the audio' is inaccurate. A transmitted 38 kHz carrier lies far above the 15 kHz audio band, so it would never be heard in the audio; a mono receiver's low-pass already removes it. The real penalties are wasted power in the carrier and the need to separate the carrier cleanly before detection.
fix: A transmitted 38 kHz carrier would use up most of the power in the difference channel while carrying no information, and the receiver would need extra filtering to keep it from biasing the difference detector. Suppressing it and sending a small 19 kHz pilot is far cheaper in power, and the pilot is doubled back to 38 kHz with the correct phase.
